RMG exports increase in Q1’FY27
item.description:
The country's ready-made garment (RMG) exports have increased. However, a major portion of this growth stems from products that have traditionally topped Bangladesh's export list.
In contrast, the export of relatively high-value garments is growing slowly, with exports of certain product categories even declining.
As a result, despite the rise in overall export earnings, little progress has been made in product diversification and increasing the share of high-value garments.
This picture emerged from an analysis of Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) data compiled by Mohiuddin Rubel, founder and CEO of Bangladesh Apparel Voice (BAV).
According to the data, during the first quarter (July–September) of the current FY27, RMG exports reached $10.58 billion.
In the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year, exports stood at $9.97 billion. Accordingly, exports grew by 6.10% or $608 million.
The analysis by BAV's CEO shows that $573 million of this export growth came from basic apparel—meaning nearly 94% of the total export growth was driven by this category.
During this period, basic apparel exports rose by 7.45% to reach $8.26 billion.
The share of basic garments in total RMG exports also expanded, rising to 78.06% from 77.08% in the first quarter of the previous year.
Among basic apparel, the largest contributors to export growth were trousers/pants, sweaters & cardigans, and t-shirts & vests.
Export earnings from these three product categories increased by $201 million, $178 million, and $104 million, respectively.
Combined, these three items accounted for nearly 80% of total export growth.
Meanwhile, children's wear recorded the highest growth rate at 10.19%, though total exports in this category stood at $300 million.
On the other hand, exports of semi-basic apparel saw only modest growth.
This category includes shirts and blouses.
In the first quarter, exports of these items grew by 1.77% to $842 million. Their share in total exports dropped from 8.30% last year to 7.96%.
The picture for high-value apparel is even weaker. Exports of high-end garments increased by just 1.42%, reaching $1.48 billion—a mere $21 million increase over the previous year.
Outerwear exports (coats, jackets, blazers, and overcoats) increased by just $33 million, while technical apparel grew by $18 million.
However, exports of gown-type apparel (frocks, long gowns, or one-piece women's wear) fell by 10.66%, sportswear & activewear dropped by 11.24%, and suits & ensembles declined by 14.48%.
Consequently, the share of high-end garments in total RMG exports contracted from 14.63% to 13.98%.

item.title: Bangladesh’s LDC graduation postponed by 3 years to November 2029
item.description:
Bangladesh’s graduation from the least developed country (LDC) category has been postponed by another three years. Instead of 24 November 2026, the country will now graduate in November 2029. This gives Bangladesh an additional three years to prepare.

The decision was approved at a plenary meeting of the United Nations General Assembly, which began at 1:00 am today, Friday. The meeting was chaired by UN General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman. UN Web TV broadcast the meeting live.

At the beginning of the meeting, Uruguay’s representative, speaking on behalf of the G-77, tabled a draft proposal to defer the LDC graduation of Bangladesh and Nepal by three years. No country’s representative opposed the proposal.

Representatives of France, Canada and Ireland, the latter speaking on behalf of the European Union, expressed support for postponing the graduation of Bangladesh and Nepal. However, all of them called for reforms in Bangladesh in their statements.

Bangladesh’s preparations for LDC graduation weak: UN report
Bangladesh was scheduled to graduate from the list of least developed countries on 24 November 2026. Following graduation, Bangladesh would become a fully-fledged developing country.

On 21 July, the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) recommended that the UN General Assembly take the final decision on Bangladesh’s request for an extension of its preparatory period for LDC greaduation.

Earlier, after reviewing Bangladesh’s application, the UN Committee for Development Policy (CDP) had recommended that the request by Bangladesh and Nepal to extend their preparatory periods be placed before the General Assembly for consideration. Based on that recommendation, ECOSOC decided to refer the matter to the General Assembly.

The final decision to extend the LDC preparatory period was taken today.

Bangladesh was scheduled to graduate from the list of least developed countries on 24 November 2026. Following graduation, Bangladesh would become a fully-fledged developing country.

The United Nations divides its member states into two categories: developed and developing countries. Countries on the LDC list are also developing countries. Those that lag behind other developing countries and require assistance from other nations are classified as least developed countries.

In 2021, the CDP made its final recommendation that Bangladesh graduate from the LDC category in 2024. However, the graduation was deferred by two years because of the Covid-19 pandemic.

Why the request for postponement

The policy of remaining firm on Bangladesh’s graduation from the least developed country (LDC) category in 2026 continued till the tenure of the interim government led by Professor Muhammad Yunus. However, after the BNP government took office in February this year, Bangladesh formally applied for a three-year postponement of its graduation from the LDC list.

The government argued that an extension would provide the necessary policy space to stabilise the macroeconomy, consolidate ongoing reforms, and complete priority activities under the Smooth Transition Strategy (STS).

Bangladesh’s letter also stated that the five-year preparatory period for LDC graduation had been ‘severely disrupted’ by a series of domestic and international crises.

Global crises included the lingering effects of the Covid-19 pandemic, a slow global economic recovery, the Russia-Ukraine war and the resulting volatility in energy and food markets, tighter global financial conditions, delays in the recovery of trade, instability in the Middle East and growing uncertainty in the global trading system.

Domestic challenges included irregularities in the financial sector, the political transition following the mass uprising of 2024, and the unresolved repatriation of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar.

LDC graduation: What needs to be done after applying for an extension

Bangladesh’s position

Bangladesh was included in the list of least developed countries (LDCs) in 1975. As an LDC, it has since enjoyed various benefits, including duty-free access for its exports. The United Nations Committee for Development Policy (CDP) makes recommendations on which countries should graduate from the LDC category.

LDCs are assessed every three years. A country’s eligibility for graduation is determined on the basis of three indicators: per capita income, human assets, and climate and economic vulnerability. A country must meet the thresholds for any two of the three indicators, or its per capita income must be twice the required threshold. These criteria, however, change over time.

Bangladesh met the thresholds for all three indicators in the 2018 and 2021 triennial reviews. These are gross national income (GNI), the Human Assets Index (HAI) and the Economic Vulnerability Index (EVI).

In 2021, the CDP made its final recommendation that Bangladesh graduate from the LDC category in 2024. However, the graduation was deferred by two years because of the Covid-19 pandemic; otherwise, Bangladesh would have graduated two years earlier. Now, a further three years have been added to the preparatory period for graduation.

item.title: A watershed moment: Bangladesh joins the global fight against rice methane
item.description:
This past week, I attended an event in Dhaka that will likely go down in history as a watershed moment for Bangladesh. Our country formally joined a global movement to rein in methane emissions, particularly from the agricultural sector.
With the next UN Climate Change Conference, COP31, scheduled for November 9-20, 2026, the timing could not be more opportune. This strategic move allows Bangladesh to arrive on the global stage with a powerful, demonstrable commitment to curbing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.
On Tuesday, Bangladesh formally joined AcceLER (Accelerating Scaling of Low-Emissions Rice in Southeast Asia). The initiative is designed to help countries plan, implement, and track effective methane mitigation measures.
Through a combination of suitability mapping, robust monitoring systems, remote sensing, and institutional capacity building, several major Asian rice-producing economies -- including Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, the Philippines, and Indonesia -- are already benefiting from the program. Now, Bangladesh joins their ranks, aiming to substantially reduce the climate impact of its paddy fields.
Rice occupies three-fourths of Bangladesh’s cultivated land. It remains fundamental to national food security, rural employment, and smallholder livelihoods.
The irrigated Boro rice ecosystem is the country's most productive agricultural system, supplying about 55% of domestic production between December and May. However, its heavy reliance on groundwater and prolonged flooding makes it a major source of methane emissions.
Methane emissions from rice cultivation in Bangladesh are estimated at 32.4 MtCO₂e (million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent), making rice one of the country's largest sources of methane.
To put this figure into perspective, 32.4 MtCO₂e is roughly equivalent to the annual greenhouse gas emissions of 7.7 million gasoline-powered passenger vehicles, the annual electricity consumption of 6.3 million homes, or the amount of carbon sequestered by 535 million tree seedlings grown for a decade.
Methane is an extremely potent super-pollutant -- 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide over a 20-year period -- which means curbing these emissions can help prevent catastrophic climate change.
It is responsible for about 30% of recent global warming. Furthermore, methane contributes to the formation of ground-level ozone, which harms human health and reduces crop yields. Cutting methane emissions is among the fastest and most effective ways to slow the rise in global temperatures.
The primary driver of these high emissions is the continuous presence of irrigation water in rice fields. Over the decades, well-intentioned initiatives, such as canal excavation and heavily subsidized irrigation water pumped through tube wells, have entrenched farming practices that rely on prolonged flooding. Continuously flooding croplands during the dry Boro season has come at a considerable environmental cost.
Today, this agricultural system faces growing challenges from declining groundwater levels, soaring irrigation costs, high energy consumption, and severe climate risks.
Fortunately, practical solutions exist. Water-saving practices, such as alternate wetting and drying (AWD), improved nutrient management through techniques like fertilizer deep placement, direct seeded rice (DSR), and short-duration rice varieties, can significantly reduce emissions by limiting the prolonged oxygen-deprived conditions that encourage methane-producing bacteria.
Instead of keeping fields permanently flooded, AWD requires farmers to allow water levels to fall periodically, exposing the soil to air. The resulting influx of oxygen suppresses methane production, significantly reducing emissions while conserving increasingly depleted groundwater resources.
Historically, methane emissions have been difficult to measure, making it challenging for governments to take effective action. Today, advanced satellite technologies offer greater transparency, helping authorities identify emission sources more accurately.
Since about 60% of methane emissions come from human activities, access to open, reliable data is essential for policymakers, scientists, and industry leaders to collaborate across borders.
Building on these technological advances, the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) recently brought together government agencies, researchers, and development partners in Dhaka to strengthen Bangladesh's capacity for the measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) of agricultural greenhouse gas emissions.
Dr Humnath Bhandari, who has headed IRRI's operations in Bangladesh for many years, highlighted digital MRV as a promising, affordable, and accurate way to track progress on a large scale. By mapping the extent to which farmers have adopted low-methane technologies, authorities can design more targeted and effective interventions.
Bangladesh can draw inspiration from its neighbours. On the sidelines of the Dhaka event, Dr Bjoern Ole Sander, an IRRI senior scientist and climate change mitigation team lead who heads the institute's operations in Thailand, shared how the organization has helped millions of Thai farmers transition to low-emission rice production across 100,000 hectares in six provinces.
While Thailand is a net rice exporter, Bangladesh remains structurally vulnerable. Despite being the world's third-largest rice producer, the country frequently relies on imports because of its high per capita rice consumption and a population that grows by around two million people annually. This vulnerability is compounded by crop losses caused by floods and other disasters.
Scaling up science-based, transparent low-emission practices is no longer optional; it is a priority for the country's long-term food security and climate resilience. By successfully implementing the AcceLER initiative, Bangladesh stands to reap significant benefits:
Transitioning to cleaner farming practices could also contribute to more liveable cities and healthier, more resilient communities across the country. The tools are available, the framework is in place, and the timing is right.
The challenge now is for Bangladesh's agricultural extension services to have the capacity and commitment to bring these practical, water-saving technologies out of the laboratories and into farmers' fields.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Biman forms probe body over technical glitch on PM's flight
item.description:
Biman Bangladesh Airlines has formed an investigation committee to determine the cause of a technical malfunction that delayed a flight carrying Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and his entourage in Japan.
Shahnur Ahmed, general manager of Biman's public relations department, confirmed the development to Dhaka Tribune on Friday.
He said the airline had formed an internal committee under its standard procedure for investigating such incidents and instructed it to submit its findings promptly.
The committee will be headed by Biman's Chief of Planning and Scheduling. Its members include the chief engineer (Engineering Production), deputy chief (Flight Safety) and manager (Legal Affairs), who will serve as member secretary.
The committee has been tasked with identifying the cause and nature of the malfunction, reviewing the measures taken to ensure the aircraft's airworthiness, and assessing the impact on flight schedules, passengers and the airline's reputation.
It will submit its report to Biman's managing director and chief executive officer.
Flight BG377, carrying the prime minister and his entourage, departed Narita International Airport in Japan five and a half hours behind schedule due to the technical glitch.
Biman's engineering team and Japanese technicians completed the repairs. The aircraft was pushed back at 7:43pm Bangladesh time and departed for Dhaka at 7:55pm.

item.title: Bangladesh wins three more years before LDC graduation
item.description:
Bangladesh has secured three more years to prepare for its graduation from the United Nations’ least developed country (LDC) category, pushing the deadline from November 24, 2026, to November 24, 2029, and giving the country crucial time to protect its export competitiveness and address longstanding economic weaknesses.
The UN General Assembly approved the extension on Thursday following a proposal introduced by Uruguay on behalf of Bangladesh and Nepal, with the backing of the Group of 77 and China.
The decision followed a favourable assessment by the UN Committee for Development Policy (CDP) and a recommendation from the UN Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC).
Bangladesh had sought the extension amid mounting economic pressures, including global trade uncertainty, energy supply disruptions, sluggish investment and persistent weaknesses in its banking and industrial sectors.
Although Bangladesh has already met all three UN criteria for LDC graduation, the government argued that additional preparation time was necessary to manage the transition without exposing its export industries to sudden competitive disadvantages.
The extended period will allow Bangladesh to pursue new trade agreements, strengthen industrial productivity, diversify exports and undertake reforms aimed at improving its competitiveness after graduation.
The most immediate concern is the future of Bangladesh’s export trade, particularly the ready-made garment industry, which accounts for the overwhelming majority of the country’s merchandise export earnings.
As an LDC, Bangladesh enjoys duty-free and quota-free access to several international markets, including the European Union under its Everything But Arms arrangement.
Graduation would begin the process of withdrawing some of these benefits, although the timing would vary according to the rules of individual trading partners.
Under the EU’s current arrangements, graduating countries generally receive a three-year transition period before losing LDC-specific preferences.
Without an alternative trade arrangement, Bangladeshi garment exporters could eventually face tariffs of around 12% in the EU market, weakening their competitiveness against countries enjoying preferential access.
A three-year delay in graduation could therefore provide additional time to secure trade agreements and prepare businesses for tougher competition.
However, extending LDC status would not guarantee that every existing benefit remains unchanged, as trade preferences and financing arrangements are governed by separate rules.
Bangladesh formally requested the extension in February 2026, citing the lingering effects of the pandemic, geopolitical conflicts, international trade uncertainty and pressure on energy supplies.
The CDP subsequently concluded that an extension would be appropriate, provided Bangladesh made substantial progress in addressing its structural vulnerabilities.
In July, ECOSOC recommended that the General Assembly consider the request before the existing graduation deadline.
The UN assessment identified financial-sector instability, weak domestic revenue mobilisation, limited export diversification and inadequate productive capacity among the areas requiring urgent attention.
These problems have persisted despite Bangladesh’s progress in meeting the economic and social indicators for graduation.
The additional period, if approved, would give policymakers more time to strengthen the banking system, increase tax revenue, improve infrastructure and reduce the cost of doing business.
The government has been pursuing bilateral and regional trade arrangements to protect market access after graduation.
Commerce, Industries and Textiles and Jute Minister Khandaker Abdul Muktadir has said the government aims to conclude comprehensive economic partnership or free trade agreements with eight to ten countries during 2026–27.
Bangladesh is also exploring closer trade arrangements with the European Union and opportunities under the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership.
The government has identified lengthy licensing procedures, regulatory delays and unreliable energy supplies as obstacles to investment and industrial expansion.
Proposed measures include digitalising business registration, streamlining licensing and improving coordination among regulatory agencies.
But trade agreements alone will not resolve the country’s competitiveness challenges. Exporters will also need to improve productivity, diversify products and comply with international labour, environmental and rules-of-origin requirements.
The UN’s assessments have made clear that any additional preparation period must be used to accelerate reforms rather than postpone difficult decisions.
Bangladesh would be expected to make measurable progress under its national smooth transition strategy, including financial-sector reform, revenue mobilisation and export diversification.
The government has maintained that it remains committed to graduating from LDC status and views the extension as a means of ensuring a sustainable transition.
For Bangladesh’s exporters, the stakes are substantial. An additional three years could create room to negotiate better market access and improve industrial capacity.
But the longer-term outcome will depend on whether that time produces meaningful reforms before the country eventually loses its LDC-specific advantages.

item.title: Major fluctuations in HSC results over 36 yrs: A year-by-year breakdown of pass rates
item.description:
The results of this year’s Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations will be published tomorrow, Saturday (31 October). Looking back at the examination performance over the past 36 years ahead of the announcement, the pass rate has undergone significant fluctuations.

In some years, the pass rate plummeted below 25 per cent, while in others, it exceeded 75 per cent. In 2020, owing to the COVID-19 pandemic, all candidates were declared successful through an alternative evaluation without sitting examinations, resulting in a 100 per cent pass rate.

These fluctuations in pass rates not only highlight shifts in student performance but also raise fundamental questions regarding the various parameters that influence examination outcomes.

Factors such as question design, script evaluation, candidate preparation, syllabus coverage, and assessment methodologies can all impact final results. However, pass rate statistics alone cannot definitively quantify the exact weight of each individual factor.

According to a prior announcement, the results for this year’s HSC and equivalent examinations were scheduled for release on 29 October. The date was subsequently rescheduled to 31 October.

This year’s HSC and equivalent examinations commenced on 2 July. A total of 1,270,583 regular and irregular candidates sat for the examinations, though a notable number of registered candidates were absent.

sharp decline in pass rate last year

An analysis of HSC examination results from 1990 to 2025 reveals that the lowest pass rate during this period occurred in 1996, at 24.77 per cent. Conversely, during the pandemic in 2020, the pass rate reached an all-time high of 100 per cent. However, the 2020 result cannot be directly compared to outcomes derived from regular examinations, as all candidates passed under an assessment scheme conducted without exams.

In recent years, the most significant drop in pass rates occurred last year. In 2024, the average pass rate across the nine general education boards stood at 75.56 per cent. In 2025, this figure dropped sharply to 57.12 per cent—a decline of nearly 18 percentage points within a single year. Last year's performance represented the lowest pass rate recorded since 2005.

Prior to that, the pass rate in 2005 stood at 59.16 per cent. Over the subsequent years, pass rates gradually increased, though this growth was not uniform and experienced occasional dips. Eventually, pass rates oscillated within the 60 to 70 per cent range.

To comprehend the cause of last year’s steep decline, a simple year-on-year comparison is insufficient. Education experts note that script evaluation standards, subject-specific outcomes, student preparation, and question design played critical roles.

An analysis following last year's result publication indicated a higher failure rate in English and Information and Communication Technology (ICT), which dragged down the overall average.

Whether this year’s results mark a recovery or continue the downward trend observed last year will be revealed on Saturday.

Historically low pass rates in early decades

The analysis over 36 years shows that in 1990, the HSC pass rate stood at 29.70 per cent. It rose over the following two years to roughly 51 per cent in 1991 and over 65 per cent in 1992, before dropping again. The pass rate was just above 46 per cent in 1993, over 40 per cent in 1994, and over 46 per cent in 1995.

A major slump occurred in 1996, when the pass rate fell to 24.77 per cent. Although pass rates fluctuated upwards over the next few years, consistency remained elusive. The pass rate stood at over 39 per cent in 1997, over 28 per cent in 2001, and approximately 27 per cent in 2002. It rose to over 38 per cent in 2003 and reached nearly 48 per cent in 2004.

In 2005, the pass rate climbed past 59 per cent, maintaining an upward trajectory over the next few years. The pass rate stood at nearly 64 per cent in 2006, over 64 per cent in 2007, and nearly 75 per cent in 2008, before dropping slightly to just over 70 per cent in 2009. In 2010 and 2011, pass rates hovered around 72 per cent, rising above 76 per cent in 2012.

Oscillating around the 70pc mark

Following 2012, the HSC pass rate hovered around 70 per cent for several years. It recorded over 71 per cent in 2013 and nearly 76 per cent in 2014, before declining to roughly 66 per cent in 2015.

The pass rate rebounded to over 72 per cent in 2016, then fell to nearly 67 per cent in 2017, roughly 65 per cent in 2018, and close to 72 per cent in 2019.

Data from this era shows that pass rates did not follow a single trajectory. Increases in one year were often followed by declines in the next, or returned to previous baselines. Consequently, a single year’s pass rate cannot serve as the sole benchmark for measuring the quality of the broader education system.

Alongside pass rates, factors such as learning quality, subject-specific proficiency, and evaluation methods must also be evaluated.

100pc during the pandemic, followed by a downturn

In 2020, HSC examinations were suspended due to the COVID-19 pandemic, and all candidates were declared passed, resulting in a 100 per cent pass rate.

The following year, in 2021, the pass rate stood at 95.57 per cent, declining to 84.31 per cent in 2022. The downward trend continued, with the pass rate dropping to roughly 76 per cent in 2023 and over 75 per cent in 2024, before falling to the 57 per cent range in 2025.

Overall, HSC pass rates between 1990 and 2025 have seen repeated cycles of growth and decline. However, with last year's drop to the 57 per cent mark, anticipation surrounding this year's results remains high. Stakeholders will have to wait until 31 October to learn the final figures.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, Professor Syed Akhteruzzaman, Chairman of the Dhaka Education Board and President of the Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee, noted that HSC pass rates have fluctuated due to a variety of factors.

According to him, policy shifts over the past two years have also influenced outcomes.

He expressed hope that if merit-based, authentic evaluation standards are maintained, pass rates will gradually improve over time.

item.title: Nahid: Tarique Rahman came from London with plans for corruption, extortion
item.description:
National Citizen Party (NCP) Convener and Opposition Chief Whip Nahid Islam has accused Prime Minister Tarique Rahman of having no plan to govern the country, alleging that he returned from London with plans for corruption, plundering, extortion and land grabbing.
Speaking as the chief guest at a mass protest rally organized by the NCP's Dhaka North and South units in front of the National Museum in Shahbagh on Friday afternoon, Nahid said: “Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has no plan to run the country. Instead of addressing people's problems, he has come from London with plans for corruption, plundering, extortion and land grabbing.”
He also accused the BNP government of failing to fulfill its commitments under the July Charter, the 31-point agenda and its election manifesto.
“After thousands of people shed their blood, we ousted one autocrat. Now we are witnessing the rise of a new autocrat. We will defeat both the fallen autocrat and this new autocrat,” he said.
Nahid said NCP leaders had visited different parts of the capital over the past week and spoken to residents about their problems. They found that many households had no gas, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) cylinder prices had increased, and people were struggling with rising commodity prices.
He added that shopkeepers and small business owners were living in fear of extortion and terrorism. Electricity and gas shortages, politicization of various state institutions and deteriorating law and order were also affecting public safety.
The NCP convener accused the home minister of focusing on the constitution instead of carrying out his responsibilities. He alleged that an initiative had been taken to amend the constitution unilaterally, disregarding the July Charter and the public mandate expressed through the referendum.
Claiming that 70% of voters had supported reforms in the referendum, Nahid demanded the cancellation of the unilateral constitutional amendment committee and the formation of a Constitution Reform Council.
He said both the home minister and the energy minister had failed to perform their respective responsibilities and must take accountability for their failures. Otherwise, he warned, the movement would spread across the country.
Referring to discussions about the fallen Awami League autocrat potentially returning to the country next December, Nahid said the current government would not be able to confront the Awami League.
He also said the BNP had failed to protect the people of Bangladesh from the Awami League during its 16 years in power. Calling on young people to unite, he urged them to stand against both fascist forces and the current government.
Nahid also raised concerns over the killing of Bangladeshi citizens along the border and unrest in the hills. He referred to the persecution of Muslims in India's Assam and West Bengal and the demolition of mosques in Delhi.
Mentioning Felani Khatun and Swarna Das in connection with border killings, he alleged that more than 10 Bangladeshi citizens had been killed during the tenure of the current government.
Nahid warned that people would not accept any initiative to establish an illegal corridor through Bangladesh in connection with India. He also said people would return to the streets if Bangladesh's fair share of water was not ensured under the Ganges Water Sharing Treaty.

item.title: RNPP starts generating power; begins internal use
item.description:
The first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant (RNPP) on Friday commenced power start-up operations and began to be used internally.
"Power start-up operations for Unit-1 commenced this morning after getting permission on Thursday," Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) Chairman Mahmudul Hasan told BSS.
He said the BAERA granted start-up permission on Thursday, following which the authorities began tests for power generation, adding: “We seek everyone's prayers for the successful commencement of electricity generation at the plant.”
The chairman said that the generated electricity is being used for internal activities.
“We are currently conducting a turbine check, which will continue. Once power generation reaches 300 megawatts (MW), another inspection will be carried out. If everything is found satisfactory, permission will be granted to supply electricity to the national grid,” he said.
According to the RNPP project, Unit 1 would have to attain one more certification, named D, before supplying first nuclear power to the national grid.
It will take 15 to 20 days to reach the next level of power supply to the national grid on a trial basis, the project details said.
According to Russian Rosatom, it had begun supplying nuclear fuel for the initial loading of the VVER-1200 reactor at Unit-2 of RNPP.
Before connecting to the national grid and subsequent trial commercial operations, the unit must undergo further power ascension tests and obtain the necessary regulatory approvals, it said.
The long-awaited achievement is also expected to strengthen Bangladesh's efforts to diversify its energy mix and ensure a more stable long-term electricity supply.
RNPP, Bangladesh's first nuclear power plant, comprises two Russian-designed Generation III+ VVER-1200 reactors with a combined generating capacity of 2,400MW.
Rosatom's Engineering Division serves as the general designer and general contractor of the project.
Once Rooppur starts supplying power to the grid, Bangladesh will become the world's 33rd nuclear power-producing nation, opening a new chapter in the country's energy security and technological advancement.

item.title: HSC, equivalent exam results to be published on Saturday
item.description:
The results of this year's Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations, in which more than 12.70 lakh examinees took part, will be published on Saturday.
The results will be formally announced at 11am at the meeting room of the Secondary and Higher Education Division of the Ministry of Education.
Education and Primary and Mass Education Minister Dr A N M Ehsanul Hoque Milon will unveil the result publication activities as the chief guest.
Prime Minister's Adviser on Education and Primary and Mass Education Mahdi Amin, secretaries of the two divisions of the Education Ministry, chairmen of all boards and officials of the ministry and the boards concerned with examinations will be present at the ceremony.
Right after the unveil, examinees will be able to know their results simultaneously through their educational institutions, designated websites and SMS.
Online results can be accessed using roll and registration numbers through https://eduboardresults.gov.bd and https://educationboardresults.gov.bd
Results can also be known instantly by sending an SMS to 16140 from any mobile operator in the prescribed format.
The HSC and equivalent examinations began simultaneously across the country on July 2 under nine general education boards, the Bangladesh Technical Education Board and the Bangladesh Madrasah Education Board.
Although the written examinations were scheduled to end on August 8, some exams of several boards, including Chattogram, were postponed due to natural disasters and floods and held later. The practical examinations were completed by August 15.
The Education Ministry said a total of 12,70,583 examinees took part in the examinations under 11 boards this year. Of them, 6,21,969 were boys and 6,48,614 were girls. This year, 26,645 more girls than boys sat for the HSC examinations.
Students of 9,439 educational institutions took part in the examinations at 2,697 centers across the country.
This year, the examinations were held under a uniform question paper in the nine general education boards. A total of 10,69,714 examinees took part in the nine boards.
Meanwhile, an Inter-Education Board press release said applications for reassessment of answer scripts by students dissatisfied with their results will start from November 1.
Students can apply online until November 7. Detailed instructions will be published on the websites of the respective education boards.

item.title: Bangladesh issues new e-rickshaw rules, makes registration mandatory
item.description:
Battery-powered rickshaws will no longer be allowed to operate in city corporation areas without registration under new government regulations aimed at bringing discipline to urban transport.
The regulations make registration mandatory for e-rickshaws across all city corporation areas, including Dhaka, introducing a formal requirement for their operation.
The Local Government Division under the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives issued a notification on Thursday, October 29, introducing the Three-Wheeled Slow-Speed Battery-Operated Rickshaw (E-Rickshaw) Operation Rules, 2026.
Issued under Section 120 of the Local Government (City Corporation) Act, 2009, the rules apply to e-rickshaws operating in all city corporation areas. No vehicle can operate without registration, a fitness certificate and compliance with technical and safety standards set by the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET).
Applicants must submit the prescribed application form, supporting documents and applicable fees to the relevant authority. Authorities will assess applications against BUET's technical and safety standards and, if satisfied, complete registration within 30 working days of receiving an application.
Each registered vehicle will receive a unique registration number containing a QR code and a number plate. The QR-coded registration number must be displayed prominently.
Registration certificates will remain valid for 5 years. If an application is rejected, the authority must notify the applicant in writing, stating the reasons, within 7 working days.
An aggrieved applicant may appeal to the higher authority within 10 working days of receiving the rejection order. The decision on the appeal will be final.
An individual may register up to 5 e-rickshaws across one or more city corporations using a single national identity card. However, a vehicle registered in one city corporation cannot operate commercially in another.
No e-rickshaw can be registered or have its registration renewed without a fitness certificate issued in accordance with BUET's technical and safety specifications and countersigned by the relevant traffic department.
Authorities responsible for issuing fitness certificates and providing countersignatures must maintain separate registration records.
Existing e-rickshaws may also be brought under the regulations after structural modifications to meet BUET's technical and safety requirements. They must subsequently obtain fitness certificates countersigned by the relevant traffic department.
The government plans to gradually bring e-rickshaws under insurance coverage.
Each vehicle will have an economic lifespan of 12 years from its registration date. After that period, its registration and number plate must be canceled.
Speedometers or odometers will be mandatory, while unregistered, defective or unsafe vehicles cannot operate.
If a mechanical defect is detected, the vehicle must immediately display a visible sign at the front stating that it is unfit to operate because of the mechanical fault. Arrangements must also be made for repairs.
Traffic departments, law enforcement agencies and designated executive magistrates will be authorized to take joint or separate action to stop the operation of illegal e-rickshaws.
E-rickshaws will be prohibited from operating on national highways, expressways, elevated expressways, major bus routes and corridors, as well as other roads restricted by the authorities from time to time. They will also be prohibited from using footpaths.
Drivers must keep to the left lane, avoid irregular overtaking and lane changes, and refrain from using mobile phones while driving.
Depending on their size, vehicles may carry a maximum of 2 or 4 passengers, excluding the driver.
E-rickshaws cannot transport commercial goods, except passengers' hand-carried belongings. Horns exceeding 40 decibels are also prohibited.
The maximum permitted speed around schools, hospitals, religious institutions and crowded public places will be 15 kilometers per hour.
City corporations and traffic departments will jointly determine designated routes for e-rickshaws and organize them by zones. Vehicles registered or authorized for one zone cannot operate in another.
The authorities will jointly determine the number of e-rickshaws permitted in each zone, designated roads and specific color codes to facilitate identification and traffic management.
City corporations, in consultation with traffic departments, will arrange designated parking facilities in every ward or other suitable locations.
Authorities may also arrange driver training through recognized institutions, covering traffic laws, road safety, battery and vehicle maintenance, and other relevant issues.
The regulations bring e-rickshaw charging under a formal licensing and monitoring system while encouraging renewable energy use.
Batteries may be charged only at charging points or designated garages approved by the relevant authority and licensed by the respective city corporation. These facilities must introduce renewable energy or solar power systems.
Authorities will take initiatives to establish approved charging stations, garages and battery-swapping centers through public-private partnerships, private investment or other arrangements, in consultation with local electricity distribution authorities and traffic departments.
The rules also encourage solar-powered charging through net metering. Under this arrangement, charging stations may supply surplus electricity generated by solar panels to the national grid during the day and draw electricity from the grid at night to charge batteries.
Government approval will be mandatory for establishing charging stations. Illegal electricity connections or unauthorized electricity consumption for battery charging will be punishable under existing laws.
Government and autonomous bodies, private institutions, scheduled banks and financial companies may provide loans to e-rickshaw owners and drivers to purchase vehicles meeting approved standards and develop supporting infrastructure.
The regulations require compliance with the Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act, 1995, related rules and government directives throughout the production, import, use, recycling and management of e-rickshaws and their batteries.
Individuals and organizations cannot dump old or unusable batteries, or parts of them, in open spaces, soil, water bodies or ordinary waste streams. Burning such batteries is also prohibited.
The regulations establish a formal framework for e-rickshaw operations, covering registration, vehicle safety, traffic management, charging infrastructure and environmental risks associated with battery disposal.

item.title: Dengue: 3 more die, 1,262 hospitalized in 24hrs
item.description:
Three people died of dengue in the last 24 hours till 8am on Friday, while 1,262 were hospitalized after being infected with the mosquito-borne disease during the same period.
The latest fatalities have raised the country's dengue death toll to 418 this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Of the newly-hospitalized dengue patients, 435 were in Dhaka Division, 75 in Mymensingh Division, 268 in Chittagong Division, 131 in Khulna Division, 112 in Rajshahi Division, 48 in Rangpur Division, 182 in Barisal Division and 11 in Sylhet Division.
According to the report, a total of 133,367 dengue patients have, so far, been hospitalized across the country this year.
So far, 126,713 dengue patients have recovered and returned home after receiving treatment in the hospitals.
A total of 102,861 people were infected with dengue, and 413 people died from the mosquito- borne disease last year.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,251 as two die in 24 hours
item.description:
Two more children died with measles symptoms in the past 24 hours, starting at 8am on Thursday.
Besides, 1,391 suspected and confirmed measles cases were reported during the same period, a press release issued by the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) said here on Friday.
With two deaths, the total number of fatalities from the suspected measles reached 1,146 since March 15, 2026, the release said.
"No one died from confirmed measles in the last 24 hours," it said, adding that a total of 105 children have died from confirmed measles since March 15.
The total number of fatalities from confirmed measles and measles-like symptoms has reached 1,251 so far, since March 15.
According to the release, 1,316 suspected measles cases were reported in the last 24 hours, while the number of suspected cases stood at 227,673 from March 15 to October 30.
Since March 15, the number of confirmed measles cases was 75 in the last 24 hours, bringing the total number of confirmed cases to 23,770.
A total of 202,639 patients with suspected measles were admitted to different hospitals across the country from March 15 to October 30. A total of 194,399 patients were discharged from the hospitals during the period.

item.title: Bangladesh, Japan stress stronger economic ties, alternative financing
item.description:
Bangladesh and Japan on Friday, underscored the need to strengthen their longstanding economic relations and expand cooperation in alternative financing to accelerate infrastructure development and deepen bilateral economic partnership.
The issue came up at a bilateral meeting between Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury and his Japanese counterpart Satsuki Katayama at the Japanese Finance Minister’s office in Tokyo, according to a finance ministry media release received on Friday.
Japanese Assistant Finance Minister Mimura Atsushi also attended the meeting, which took place in a cordial atmosphere.
During the meeting, the two sides recalled the longstanding and strong economic relations between Bangladesh and Japan and held detailed discussions on ways to take their bilateral and economic partnership to a new height, said the release.
They put special emphasis on expanding economic cooperation through alternative financing mechanisms beyond foreign direct investment (FDI), alongside infrastructure development and trade expansion.
Both sides expressed their agreement to take effective initiatives to make the existing economic partnership more dynamic and explore opportunities for cooperation in new sectors. Special Assistant to the prime minister on Investment and Capital Market Affairs Tanvir Ghani and senior officials from both countries were also present at the meeting.
Japan remains one of Bangladesh’s major development partners. Japanese financing has supported several large-scale infrastructure and social development projects in Bangladesh in the past, while the two countries continue to implement important projects and sign new agreements.

item.title: 159 Dhaka-Riyadh flights cancelled, 22,721 passengers affected
item.description:
Flight cancellations between Dhaka and Riyadh have continued amid security concerns in Saudi Arabia, with 159 flights cancelled since October 10, affecting 22,721 passengers.
Kawser Mahmud, assistant director of the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh’s (CAAB) public relations department, confirmed the figures on Friday night.
Of the cancelled flights, 82 were direct services. These included 37 operated by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, 10 by US-Bangla Airlines, 20 by Saudia and 15 by Riyadh Air.
Another 77 were transit flights, including 30 operated by IndiGo, seven by SalamAir, one by EgyptAir, 14 by Emirates, nine by Qatar Airways, eight by flydubai and eight by Air India.
The CAAB official said flight cancellations would continue until the security situation improves.

item.title: Dhaka wants Thailand to buy more of its pharma, jute products to reduce trade deficit
item.description:
Bangladesh has proposed that Thailand import more pharmaceuticals and jute products from Bangladesh and reduce duties on Bangladeshi goods to improve their competitiveness in the Thai market as part of efforts to reduce the bilateral trade gap.
The Thais, during the 4th Foreign Office Consultations (FOC) held at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Thailand on Friday, expressed willingness to consider the proposals and further expand bilateral trade and investment between the two countries.
The Thai delegation also requested the early initiation of discussions on a bilateral Free Trade Agreement (FTA).
The two sides reaffirmed their commitment to elevating bilateral relations through enhanced cooperation at bilateral, regional and international levels.
Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam led the Bangladesh delegation, while the Thai delegation was led by Permanent Secretary of the Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs Eksiri Pintaruchi.
The consultations reviewed the entire gamut of bilateral relations, including cooperation in trade and investment, connectivity, workers' migration, energy, agriculture, cultural exchanges, education and training, defence and climate change.
On connectivity, both sides welcomed the commencement of the first direct shipping service between Chittagong and Ranong ports in September 2026.
The service is expected to reduce transportation time from approximately 15 days to just four days, lowering logistics costs and boosting bilateral trade.
Bangladesh sought Thailand's technical cooperation and investment in processing Bangladeshi fruits and vegetables, as well as technology transfer to tap the global halal food market.
Under the Thailand International Cooperation Agency (TICA) programme, Bangladesh sought training for professionals in hospitality, nursing, germplasm and food processing sectors.
Thailand also stressed sharing its experience of the "One Village One Product" programme.
The two sides agreed to consider various MoUs currently under discussion, including those on rice imports and workers' migration. Both sides expressed satisfaction with the ongoing energy cooperation, said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Referring to the government's national objective of generating at least 20% of electricity from renewable sources by 2030, Bangladesh sought Thailand's technical expertise and experience in converting agricultural residues and agro-industrial waste into electricity.
Looking ahead to the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Bangladesh and Thailand next year, the two sides stressed the importance of exchanges at the political level and expressed hope that visits by the heads of government next year could mark the anniversary.
They also agreed to undertake joint initiatives to promote cultural and sports exchanges.
As part of these efforts, Bangladesh offered to share its expertise in cricket and training, while Thailand offered training in Taekwondo.
On regional and multilateral cooperation, Bangladesh appreciated Thailand's continued support for its aspiration to become an Asean Sectoral Dialogue Partner and accede to the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP).
The Bangladesh delegation also sought Thailand's support in addressing the repatriation of displaced Rohingyas to Rakhine State in Myanmar.
Both sides acknowledged the growing threat of cross-border crimes, including human and arms trafficking, online scamming and narcotics trade.
In this context, they agreed to work together and consider establishing a joint committee under their respective Ministries of Home Affairs.

West Indies crush Bangladesh by eight wickets in Mirpur Test
item.description:
West Indies defeated Bangladesh by eight wickets in the Mirpur Test on Saturday, chasing down a target of 170 with ease to take a 1-0 lead in the two-match series.

Bangladesh, led by Najmul Hossain Shanto, failed to put up a fight after setting the visitors a modest target. West Indies reached 170-2 in just 35.1 overs, with Brendon King and Kavem Hodge guiding them to victory.

King remained unbeaten on 81, while Hodge finished on 31 not out off 27 balls. John Campbell also made a valuable contribution with 49.

The ease with which West Indies chased the target was in stark contrast to Bangladesh's batting performance on the same pitch. The surface had offered considerable turn to the West Indies spinners earlier in the day, making it appear a spin-friendly wicket.

However, Bangladesh's spinners, Taijul Islam and Mehidy Hasan Miraz, failed to replicate that success. They struggled to bowl consistently in the right areas, allowing King and Campbell to attack without giving the bowlers much opportunity to settle into a rhythm.

Bangladesh had scored 272 in their first innings before being dismissed for 142 in the second. Nayeem Hasan top-scored in the second innings with 52, while Zakir Hasan contributed 22.

West Indies' spinners played a decisive role in restricting Bangladesh, with Roston Chase taking five wickets for 36 runs and Jomel Warrican claiming four for 63.

West Indies had scored 245 in their first innings, giving Bangladesh a narrow 27-run lead. But the hosts' second-innings collapse left the visitors with a target they chased down comfortably.

Hasan Mahmud took one wicket for 14 runs during West Indies' second-innings chase, but Bangladesh could not prevent the visitors from completing a convincing victory.

The result puts West Indies in the lead ahead of the second and final Test of the series on 5 November.

item.title: Saudi says intercepted ‘hostile drone’ in Riyadh region
item.description:
Saudi air defenses intercepted a drone in the Riyadh region on Saturday, according to the spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis.
“Air defenses intercepted and destroyed a hostile drone in the Riyadh region,” Turki al-Malki wrote on X, adding that “debris from the interception fell without causing injuries.”
Malki did not say who launched the drone.
In recent weeks, Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, including by launching deadly strikes on Riyadh airport that forced its closure for two weeks and the cancellation of flagship events -- threatening the kingdom’s economic diversification plans.
On Friday, Malki said the Houthis had targeted the Medina region, home to Islam’s second holiest city, but the group later denied the claim.
The Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure, airports and ships come after hostilities resumed in Yemen over the summer between the Houthis and the country’s internationally recognized government, which is backed by Riyadh.
More than 1,600 people have been killed and over 275,000 displaced since the fighting reignited, according to United Nations figures.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen’s capital Sanaa in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast in a lightning campaign.
The Houthis have reported frequent Saudi airstrikes in areas they control as Riyadh retaliates.

West Indies crush Bangladesh by eight wickets in first Test
item.description:
Brandon King struck a career-best 81 not out as West Indies cruised to an eight-wicket win over Bangladesh in the first Test on Saturday to take a 1-0 lead in the two-match series.
King hit 10 fours and a six in his 115-ball knock to help the visitors chase down the target of 170 in 35.1 overs on the fourth day in Mirpur after Bangladesh were bowled out for 142 in their second innings.
Jomel Warrican, who was named player of the match, claimed 4-63 to follow up his five-wicket haul in Bangladesh's first innings as the hosts were bowled out in 48.4 overs.
West Indies captain Roston Chase took 5-36 in the second innings, his fifth five-wicket haul in Test cricket.
Bangladesh had resumed the fourth day at 79-6, holding a lead of 106, but their hopes of setting a challenging target suffered an early blow when Jaker Ali edged Warrican to slip, where Chase took the catch.
Jaker, who scored 22 off 34 balls, was the second-highest scorer for Bangladesh in the innings.
Nayeem Hasan survived two dropped catches off Chase, on 21 and 29, to keep Bangladesh going.
He added 26 runs with Hasan Mahmud before Warrican trapped the latter lbw for eight.
Taijul Islam contributed eight in a 17-run partnership with Nayeem before Chase dismissed him to leave Bangladesh at 127-9.
Nayeem then reached his maiden Test half-century off 87 balls, with four boundaries, but his resistance ended when he attempted to hit Chase over long-on and was caught by Joshua Bishop.
He made 52 off 91 balls, while Shoriful Islam remained unbeaten on seven as Bangladesh were dismissed cheaply.
West Indies started confidently, with openers King and John Campbell continuing their aggressive approach to take the visitors to 64 without loss in 14.1 overs before rain interrupted play.
After a delay of around an hour, they added another 23 runs before bad light and lightning forced a further stoppage of 45 minutes.
King was dropped on 70 by substitute fielder Ebadot Hossain off Taijul after the break, but the opener made Bangladesh pay with his fine, unbeaten knock.
Campbell fell just short of a half-century, bowled by Shoriful for 49 off 55 balls, with six fours and a six.
The second Test will be played in Sylhet from November 5.

item.title: Iran’s supreme leader warns US, Israel against new attacks
item.description:
Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday warned the United States and Israel against returning to war, according to a written statement, following threats from the Islamic Republic’s foes of a possible resumption of strikes.
“If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it is the armed forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine the time and conditions for ending them,” said a statement attributed to Khamenei posted on his website.
The remarks came during a reported meeting between Khamenei and senior military commanders, including armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Revolutionary Guards commander Ahmad Vahidi. It was the first reported meeting between them.
Khamenei has not been publicly seen since he became supreme leader, following his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei’s killing in US-Israeli strikes at the start of the Middle East war in February.
According to the statement, Khamenei ordered the commanders to ensure that “any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response.”
It also said that Khamenei ordered the commanders to update Iran’s target list to include “all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy.”
The war began on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which swiftly responded with attacks on countries around the region.
The supreme leader’s statement came as fresh diplomatic efforts were underway to avert a resumption of fighting.
A Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran on Friday for talks with Iranian officials, after Iran reportedly received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance.
According to Iranian media, Tehran had yet to respond to the letter.

item.title: European diplomats shun Russia at G20 gathering in the US
item.description:
A Group of 20 foreign ministers’ meeting in the US city of Atlanta got off to a rocky start on Friday after top diplomats from European nations refused to take a “family photo” along with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is hosting the gathering, decided to scrap the photo before the meeting got underway because Washington didn’t want it to become a spectacle or distraction.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters before the first session on Friday that there wouldn’t “be a family photo with European partners and Mr. Lavrov together because ... there is no normalcy with Russia.”
The two-day gathering of the G20 grouping, which includes the EU, Russia, Germany, India, China, Brazil and other major countries, is meant to be a precursor to a G20 leaders summit later this December.
That G20 leaders meeting in December is set to be hosted by US President Donald Trump at his golf club in Miami.
Rubio still opened the talks by stressing unity on major issues, telling his counterparts that they were in a “critical moment.”
“We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises,” he said.
He pointed to disruptions to global energy and trade and said many were posing “severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order.”
But several countries, including the United States and Russia, are involved in separate wars. Wars in Iran and Ukraine have resulted in a spike in food prices for people around the world.
While the message is about unity and finding solutions to problems like freedom of navigation in the Black Sea and the Strait of Hormuz during the G20 meeting, the reality is that finding common ground will likely be much tougher.
Given a renewed momentum to revive talks to end the war in Ukraine, there was also interest in getting Lavrov to talk about Russia’s stance on future talks with Kyiv.
The US has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 meeting in Miami, but it’s unclear whether Russia has accepted the invitation.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has previously said that he would be open to traveling to Miami to hold talks with Putin if he were also there.
The Kremlin has so far declined direct meetings with Zelenskyy, with Russia’s Sergey Lavrov telling DW on the sidelines of the meeting that Putin is willing to meet with the Ukrainian leader if he travels to Moscow.
“President Putin said if he [Zelenskyy] is willing to meet, let him come to Moscow,” Lavrov said. “We will guarantee his safety.”
Lavrov declined to say whether Putin will attend the G20 summit this December.
Putin has not attended a G20 leaders meeting since 2019 and only attended a session virtually in 2023.
Russia has also continued with its attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent weeks, stepping up drone strikes on water and energy infrastructure.
The European Union’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said ministers at the G20 meeting were able to call out Lavrov for his “lies” at the table.
“We were talking about the big geopolitical crises, including Ukraine, and we were able to address Sergey Lavrov head-on with this,” Kallas said on the sidelines of the meeting.
“Of course, he put forward a lot of lies, a lot of false narratives that we were also able to then rebuke,” she said.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also called out Lavrov, saying, “If we are serious about our values and our interests, we must also work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine.”
Lavrov, who is under international sanctions for Russia’s war in Ukraine, was invited to the US at a time when the two countries have appeared to have fostered warmer ties.
Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia earlier this month and also waived new sanctions on Russia’s energy. The US announced the move just weeks away from the midterm elections on November 3.
Lavrov said on Friday that despite those efforts, “in practice, no real progress in relations with the US has so far been seen.”
The Trump administration has been embroiled in disputes with South Africa, having imposed visa restrictions on South Africans who it said were complicit in discriminating against white people.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year because US officials said they made a conscious choice to include only formal members of the group.
But US officials didn’t extend that invite to South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group.
“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” said Phindile Kunene, spokesperson for South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola.
With this many issues on the table, it appeared less likely that there would be a joint consensus at the end of the talks.
Instead of a final declaration, the AFP news agency reported, the meeting is expected to end on Saturday with a chair summary drafted by the US.

item.title: Mark Carney: Canada has ‘learned we are overdependent on the US’
item.description:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke to DW on Friday after talks in Montreal with European Union leaders seeking to hammer out details of a new, closer partnership between Canada and the EU.
Amid difficult negotiations with US President Donald Trump, representing Canada’s biggest trading partner, Carney said that he and his compatriots had come to realize the country was too dependent on the economic powerhouse to the south.
“The lesson we’ve taken, Canadians as a whole, is we’re overdependent on the United States. Too closely connected to the United States. And we need to build our strength here at home and diversify and deepen our partnerships with like-minded countries internationally,” Carney said.
An EU delegation led by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa held talks with Carney and other Canadian officials in Montreal on Friday.
They’re discussing the plans floated by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to forge what she called an “associate membership” — a status that does not yet exist for any other country — even as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government resists creating this label. Carney seemed to speak in its favor.
“Well, I think the advantage of what we’re doing is that a few things are absolutely clear, irrespective of the exact terminology that’s used. President von der Leyen uses associated membership. We use associated membership,” he told DW’s Katharina Kroll at Port of Montreal Tower.
“What does that mean? It means the closest possible partnership without being a full member of the European Union, because Canada is not in Europe geographically and therefore cannot have accession.” Carney said.
Asked if he was looking to create a “new transatlantic bloc without the US,” Carney said it was more about diversifying and deepening Canada’s other partnerships than excluding by far its largest trading partner.
“We’re both partners of the United States, obviously close partners, alliance partners in Nato. And there are many, many opportunities for cooperation with the United States,” he said. “But in many cases, there’ll be much deeper cooperation for Canada between Canada and Europe than Canada and the United States.”
He mentioned both existing areas of cooperation like the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta), calling it “one of the most successful free trade agreements in the world,” and also pointed to research cooperation and programs like Horizon Europe and Erasmus+ enabling student exchanges.
But Carney also pointed to areas where the two sides could seek to expand cooperation, naming areas like space technologies, artificial intelligence and critical minerals.
Despite his well-documented difficulties with Donald Trump — perhaps most crudely exemplified by Trump’s attempts to unilaterally rename Lake Ontario, or his posting AI videos imagining him as an ice hockey player beating Carney up in a fight — Carney said US-Canadian ties were too deep to be derailed by any governments or prime ministers or presidents.
“The bonds between Canadians and Americans are longstanding. They’re very strong. And big elements of that will be maintained regardless of the government in Canada, the government in the United States, the combination of the two,” he said.
Asked about the best way to deal with Trump, Carney said it was “to be direct, to be clear, to be absolutely clear about your bottom lines are.” He said it was important to show respect but also to continue to bring “the negotiations back to the core issues.”
But he said the tensions with Trump had demonstrated the need to diversify and to seek Canada’s other most natural partners around the world.
He acknowledged that no matter the nature of the talks with the EU, “the scale of the relationship with the United States” would be “very hard to replace.”
Asked if he was concerned that the talks could expose him to further tariffs or other punitive measures from the Trump administration, Carney said, “We’ve been living with this for some time.”
“There have been many justifications for trade action against Canada that the United States has had,” he said. “Our view is that all of them are unjustified under our trade agreement.”
Carney said the crucial message, also for the Trump White House, was that the talks with Brussels concerned a “positive association” and partnership “to help solve global problems” and address global challenges.
“It’s not against somebody. It’s for. It’s a positive act,” he said.

item.title: Iran warns US, Israel against new attacks after Trump, Netanyahu threats
item.description:
Iran's supreme leader on Saturday warned the United States and Israel against launching new attacks following their threats to resume strikes after crucial elections, as fears mount over a return to fighting.

The declaration came as the Islamic republic's top diplomat said there were no plans to hold talks with the United States, as indirect mediation via Qatar continues.

President Donald Trump has warned of fresh military action after the US holds midterm elections early next week, saying last weekend that he was weighing whether to "finish them off".

In Israel, which is coming off fresh elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has spoken of a "historic, one-time opportunity" to topple the Iranian government.

Polls in both countries could determine the direction of the conflict, with Israel having voted Tuesday but yet to form a new government.

"Any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response," Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei told top military commanders in a meeting, according to a statement.

Iran says discussing plan with mediators to end war, reopen Hormuz

The encounter was the first reported meeting between Khamenei and military top brass, and included armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Revolutionary Guards commander Ahmad Vahidi.

The supreme leader has not been seen publicly since before he took the helm in March after the killing of his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in US-Israeli strikes.

Khamenei also ordered commanders to update Iran's target list to include "all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy".

Iran has previously warned it would consider severing undersea cables in the Strait of Hormuz.

Petrol prices weigh on US vote

Since the initial US-Israeli strikes in February, ordinary Iranians "have been left in a state of limbo for the past year", Fariba, a Tehran housewife, told AFP.

But other residents in the Iranian capital brushed off the possible return to full-scale conflict.

"We do not fear another war. We have been at war for 48 years now," said Ebrahim, a salesman in his forties.

Since the outbreak of the war, Tehran has restricted shipping through the strategic waterway, which normally carries around one-fifth of global oil consumption.

The blockade has caused a spike in global energy prices, making the war unpopular among the US public ahead of midterm congressional elections Tuesday.

Gains for the opposition Democrats could restrict, to an extent, Trump's ability to enact policy.

Voting in Israel has left Netanyahu's political camp with the most seats in parliament but short of a majority, leaving the make-up of the next administration unclear.

'Flames of war'

The war began on 28 February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran. The Islamic republic swiftly responded with attacks on American assets in countries around the region.

Fresh diplomatic efforts are underway to avert any resumption of fighting, with Qatari mediators landing in Tehran on Friday, and US Vice President JD Vance sending a letter to Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei.

But Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday that "currently, there are no plans for meetings with American officials".

Trump rules out new Iran attack before US midterm elections

"Iran's conditions are clear, and consultations regarding them are ongoing among mediators," he said in an interview with Al Jazeera, according to the state news agency IRNA.

Qatar and Pakistan have been mediating between the warring parties, but the talks have yet to produce a lasting agreement.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Vance had sent his letter to Iran's security chief at Trump's direction in a bid to revive negotiations and avert further US strikes.

Araghchi confirmed that Iran received the letter, saying, "The American side's effort to open a dialogue and reach a broader understanding is viewed as a positive step."

But the Iranian side kept firm its warnings against further attacks.

Earlier on Saturday, army spokesman Mohammad Akaraminia said that any resumption of hostilities would only expand the scope of the war.

"The flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area," he said on social media, without elaborating.

Araghchi warned on X of an "Earth-shattering blow Iran's Powerful Armed Forces will deal against those who dare harm our people".

He said there would no longer be any "red lines".
